implementation_notes: Go has no sum type, so the variant set is modelled as an interface carrying an unexported marker method: an ordinary named type in another package cannot declare that method with the same package identity, although embedding the exported interface can promote it and is not a hard language-sealed guarantee. Each variant is a struct holding that variant's payload. Dispatch is a type switch - a runtime check - and the compiler does not verify coverage, so a default arm that panics on an unexpected type is mandatory. This is the emulation the standard library uses for syntax trees (go/ast.Stmt carries an unexported stmtNode marker and consumers switch over the concrete node types). When you want polymorphism rather than closed matching, a plain interface with methods is the better Go tool.
pitfalls: The set is only conventionally closed: an interface value can be nil, and a struct embedding the marker interface can promote the unexported method and sneak into the set, so the default arm is load-bearing.
No exhaustiveness checking - adding a variant compiles everywhere and only the runtime panic reveals the missed switch.
A type switch is dynamic dispatch; in hot paths prefer an explicit tag field and a value switch, or methods on the interface.

An unexported marker normally prevents implementations from other packages, which is the point, but it also blocks consumers from writing ordinary new variants even in tests; use an internal test package or a constructor seam.
